name: Neşri
summary:
Mevlânâ Mehmed Neşri, also commonly referred to as Neshri, was an Ottoman historian and a prominent representative of early Ottoman historiography.

Born in the late 15th century, Neşri's life is not well-documented, but it is known that he served as the chief chronicler for Sultan Bayezid II, compiling the first comprehensive history of the Ottoman Empire.

This task allowed Neşri to weave together disparate sources, including Greek and Persian texts, to create a cohesive narrative of Ottoman history. His work, which included the chronicles of Mehmed II, was widely acclaimed during his lifetime and has had a lasting impact on our understanding of the Ottoman Empire's rise to power.

Neşri's significance extends beyond his contributions to historical scholarship; he played a crucial role in shaping the Ottoman Empire's identity and cementing its place within the broader narrative of Islamic history. His work continues to influence contemporary historians and scholars, offering valuable insights into the complexities of Ottoman politics, culture, and society.

The legacy of Neşri can be seen in the many historians who followed in his footsteps, including Köhnükhalef and Tahir Fehmi, who built upon his work to create a more comprehensive understanding of Ottoman history. Today, Neşri is recognized as one of the most important figures in the development of Ottoman historiography, and his contributions continue to be felt across disciplines and borders.

In 1519, during the reign of Sultan Selim I, Neşri suffered a stroke that left him unable to write or travel. He died shortly thereafter, leaving behind a body of work that would go on to shape our understanding of the Ottoman Empire's rich history.
